Marisol walks the tideline every morning. She sells polished sea glass and fresh coconuts, and buys what the lagoon washes up.
Hand in anything you find on the festival grounds. Every item is logged and kept for its owner, and the festival pays the finder a fee.
Brannoch weighs what you drag back from the fields: war scrap, hides from the beasts of the Fangmire, ore and crystal. He pays the city's price, and sells leather and canvas for the forge.
Hyacinth keeps the Conservatory's plants. She sells the tea herbs she grows for the Rose Tea Room, and buys good flowers and herbs for the Lounge's vases.
Delphine supplies the Everbloom's florist. She sells ribbon and fresh stems, and buys flowers cut in the garden, or brought from the Greenwold.

Sound is measured in decibels (dB). Ordinary talk is about 60 dB; close to a festival's speakers it can pass 100 dB. Health and safety guidance says 85 dB is safe for about 8 hours, and every 3 dB more halves the safe time: at 100 dB it is about 15 minutes.

The decibel scale is logarithmic: each 10 dB more is ten times the sound energy, and sounds roughly twice as loud to us. Loud sound wears out the tiny hair cells in the inner ear, and they do not grow back. Foam or musicians' earplugs take about 15 to 30 dB off.
a tenth of a bel, the unit for how strong a sound is, named after Alexander Graham Bell.
The first-aid tent gives out earplugs free. Stand by the speaker stacks of the Main Stage, then walk back to the mixing desk: the further you go, the safer you are.
About how long is 100 dB safe for, by the usual guidance?
Sound travels through air at about 343 metres a second at 20 °C. People hear from about 20 Hz, a low rumble, to about 20,000 Hz, a thin whistle, and the top end fades as we get older.

A sound's wavelength is its speed divided by its frequency, so a 50 Hz bass note is about 6.9 metres long while a 5,000 Hz note is under 7 centimetres. Long waves bend round tents and people (diffraction), and air soaks up high notes faster than low ones, so from far away you mostly hear the bass.
how many times a sound wave vibrates each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Walk away from the Main Stage across the field: the cymbals fade first and the bass line is the last thing you hear.
Why does the bass carry further than the treble?
Long waves bend round things and air absorbs high notes faster
Low notes travel faster than high ones
About how fast does sound travel in air?

Mail, rings of iron linked into a shirt, was in use by the third century BC. Full suits of plate armour were worn in Europe from about 1400. A full harness weighed about 15 to 25 kilograms, less than a modern soldier's pack, and was spread over the whole body, so a fit knight could run, climb and mount a horse.

Mail stops cuts but not the force of a blow, so it was worn over a quilted padded coat, the gambeson, to soak up the shock. Plate deflects a blow by making it glance off a curved surface. Modern body armour uses layers of tough fibres and ceramic plates that spread a bullet's energy over a wide area.
a thick quilted coat, worn under mail or on its own, that cushions blows.
Look along the Armoury's racks: from the bronze age to the star weapons, every kind of armour was an answer to the weapon of its day.
About how much did a full suit of plate armour weigh?
Why was a padded gambeson worn under mail?
To soak up the shock of a blow

In the 1790s Dominique-Jean Larrey, a French army surgeon, began treating the wounded by how urgent their injuries were, not by rank, and sent light horse-drawn 'flying ambulances' onto the field. Sorting the injured this way is still called triage.

For heavy bleeding, press firmly and directly on the wound and keep pressing. For bleeding from an arm or leg that will not stop, a tourniquet goes on 5 to 7 centimetres (two or three inches) above the wound, tight enough to stop it, and the time is written down. Someone unconscious but breathing is laid in the recovery position so their airway stays open.
from the French trier, to sort: deciding who needs help first.
Watch the field medics at the Field Hospital sort the wounded by the tent door before anyone goes inside.
What is the first thing to do for a heavily bleeding wound?
Press firmly and directly on it

Mahjong took shape in China in the middle of the 1800s, under the Qing dynasty, and spread to America and Europe in the early 1920s, where it became a craze. A standard Chinese set has 144 tiles.

The set is built like a deck of cards: three suits (dots, bamboos and characters) numbered 1 to 9, four of each, plus four winds and three dragons, four of each, which makes 136, and eight flower and season tiles. Players draw and discard to build a hand of sets, so it is a game of memory, counting and odds as much as luck.
three identical tiles, one of the sets a winning hand is made of.
Sit at a Mahjong table and count the suits: 9 numbers × 4 copies × 3 suits is 108 tiles before the honours are added.
How many tiles are in a standard Chinese set?

Bingo comes from an Italian lottery game of the 1500s. It reached France in the late 1700s as le lotto, and in the 1800s German teachers used versions of it to teach spelling and sums. In 1929 an American toy seller, Edwin S. Lowe, saw a game called beano played with dried beans at a carnival in Georgia, and sold it as bingo.

In the American game there are 75 balls and a five-by-five card with a free square in the middle; in the British game there are 90 balls and tickets of three rows. Every ball is equally likely to come out, so no card is luckier than another: the more cards in play, the more chances.
the person who draws the balls and calls out the numbers.
Look at the great board in the Bingo Hall: the caller lights each number as it is drawn.
What did players first use to mark their cards at the carnival game Lowe saw?
How many balls are there in the American game?

Playing cards were used in China by the 800s, and reached Europe in the late 1300s, probably from the Mamluk lands of Egypt and Syria. The French suits used today, hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades, appeared in about 1480. Klondike solitaire is named after the Klondike gold rush in Canada's Yukon in the 1890s.

French suits caught on because they were simple shapes that could be stencilled in two colours, so cards became cheap to print. Solitaire games are called patience in Britain. Klondike is not always winnable: some deals can never come out, however well you play.
the British name for card games played alone, like Klondike and FreeCell.
Deal a game of Klondike at a solitaire table, and count the four suits as you build them up from the aces.
Roughly when did playing cards reach Europe?
What is solitaire called in Britain?

Queen Victoria wore white lace when she married in 1840, and white wedding dresses became the fashion in many countries after her. At a Hindu wedding the couple take seven steps together round a sacred fire, one vow for each step. At a Jewish wedding the couple stand under a canopy, the chuppah, and a glass is broken at the end. At a Shinto wedding in Japan the couple share sake from three cups, three sips from each.
the canopy a couple stand under at a Jewish wedding: open on all sides, like a welcoming home.
